content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has established testing guidelines to improve the diagnosis and treatment of hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted to assess the impact of point-of-care (PoC) HCV viral load (VL) testing compared to centralized laboratory-based standard-of-care approaches. The study focused on the uptake of HCV RNA testing, initiation of HCV treatment, and the turnaround time from testing to treatment initiation among individuals who tested positive for HCV antibodies (Ab). The analysis also evaluated these outcomes across various population subgroups, including people who inject drugs, homeless individuals, prisoners, people living with HIV, and the general or mixed populations. The models of care were categorized based on whether the PoC HCV VL assay was conducted at the clinic site or a remote site. Further stratification was performed based on the timing and location of testing and treatment. This review is significant as it provides insights into the effectiveness of PoC nucleic acid testing (NAT) compared to conventional laboratory-based NAT in promoting the diagnosis of HCV viremia. These findings will inform updates to WHO testing guidelines. The primary research question addressed whether PoC HCV VL testing increases the uptake of HCV VL testing and treatment and reduces the time to treatment initiation compared to standard laboratory-based NAT testing. The secondary research question explored whether the impact of PoC HCV VL testing varies across specific models of care (e.g., fully decentralized versus partially decentralized services) and among specific populations, such as stigmatized or hard-to-reach groups with limited access to care and higher rates of loss to follow-up. The study utilized a PICO framework (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcomes) to guide the analysis. The population included individuals at risk of HCV infection targeted for testing in harm-reduction settings, HIV clinics, prisons, primary care, or other community-based settings. Subgroups of interest included people who inject drugs, prisoners, people living with HIV, men who have sex with men, homeless individuals, and the general population in primary care settings. The intervention involved PoC HCV NAT viral load assays conducted on-site or in mobile units, while the comparator was laboratory-based NAT HCV viral load assays, including high-throughput lab-based assays. Key outcomes included turnaround times (e.g., from HCV antibody testing to treatment initiation) and cascade-of-care proportions (e.g., uptake of HCV VL testing among HCV Ab-positive individuals, treatment initiation among HCV RNA-positive individuals, and sustained virologic response [SVR] testing among those completing treatment). The study design included all types of studies with data on HCV cascade-of-care outcomes and/or turnaround times. The systematic review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. The protocol was registered on PROSPERO (record ID: 218239). A comprehensive search of PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science was conducted for studies using HCV PoC RNA assays published between January 1, 2016, and September 23, 2020. Additional searches included conference abstracts from key meetings, such as the European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL) International Liver Conference 2020, the International Network on Hepatitis in Substance Users (INHSU) symposia (2016–2019), and the International Viral Hepatitis Elimination Meeting (IVHEM) 2020. Relevant studies were also identified through WHO partner organizations and contacts. Original studies were included if they involved the use of HCV RNA assays suitable for PoC testing (even if conducted in a laboratory setting) and provided data on HCV cascade-of-care outcomes and/or turnaround times. Cascade-of-care outcomes were defined as data on at least two adjacent steps in the HCV care cascade, such as the proportion of individuals tested for HCV antibodies who were offered testing, the proportion of HCV Ab-positive individuals tested for HCV RNA, and the proportion of HCV RNA-positive individuals initiating treatment. Studies with a sample size of 10 or fewer for the largest denominator were excluded. Data abstraction involved extracting detailed descriptive data for each study, including location, setting, population type, population characteristics, study design, and publication type. Settings included primary health clinics, district hospitals, harm-reduction sites, and prisons. Population types included homeless individuals, people who inject drugs, prisoners, people living with HIV, and the general population. The intervention arm was the use of PoC HCV RNA assays, while the comparator arm was centralized lab-based HCV RNA testing. The PoC HCV RNA assays were further classified based on their delivery location (on-site or in mobile units) and the model of care (e.g., same site and same day for testing and treatment, same site but different day, or different site and different day). Data on quantitative outcomes, such as the uptake of HCV RNA testing and treatment initiation, as well as turnaround times, were extracted and analyzed. Median times were preferred over means for reporting turnaround times. The findings of this systematic review and meta-analysis provide critical insights into the effectiveness of PoC HCV VL testing in improving the HCV care cascade and reducing delays in treatment initiation. These results will contribute to the development of updated WHO testing guidelines to enhance the diagnosis and treatment of HCV infections globally.
